questions.title: Resection after nodal or distant disease responds
questions.question: When perihilar cholangiocarcinoma has regional, para-aortic or distant disease that responds, when is resection reasonable?
questions.proposal: Regional nodal disease goes to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and then resection in responders, recognizing that a survival benefit is not established. Para-aortic or other non-regional nodes are not resected upfront; after durable response with negative re-sampling, MDT case-by-case only. Distant metastasis stays systemic-therapy-led; conversion only exceptionally. Any nodal disease still excludes transplantation (pCCA-B1).
rules: Regional nodes: FDG-PET-positive or tissue-proven regional nodes → neoadjuvant chemotherapy, restaging, resection if no distant disease.
Para-aortic nodes: upfront data conflict; do not resect when known. After response, consider only with negative intraoperative sampling.
Distant metastasis: systemic therapy (gemcitabine–cisplatin-based); conversion only within a registry.
questions.rationale: Upfront series disagree on para-aortic nodes, and no pCCA-specific post-response series exists (only 5 mixed-subsite para-aortic cases). Japanese conversion data are mixed biliary cancers.

studies.population: Single centre, 110 pCCA; 72 received neoadjuvant gemcitabine–S-1. Regional nodes defined by FDG-PET uptake only; distant disease excluded.
studies.results: Curative resection 85.1%, 65.8% and 24.0% in resectable, borderline and locally advanced groups.
studies.limits: No survival for node-positive patients; benefit not established.
studies.locator: Cancers 2026; Methods 2.3, Results.

studies.population: Single centre, 20 conversions of biliary cancer. 5 with para-aortic nodes; all 5 were negative on para-aortic sampling at conversion resection (in 3 the nodes had disappeared on imaging).
studies.results: One pCCA patient (para-aortic nodes cleared) had axial nodal recurrence 11 months after conversion.
studies.limits: Mixed subsites.
studies.locator: Cancers 2025; Results 3.3.

studies.population: Single centre, 143 with intraoperative para-aortic sampling. Upfront surgery.
studies.results: Para-aortic metastasis in 17 (11.9%); PET identified only 17.6%; with para-aortic metastasis, survival did not differ with or without resection (15.6 vs 18.0 months, p=0.790).
studies.limits: Not post-response.
studies.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2026 (abstract; full text pending).

studies.population: Single centre, 410 resected extrahepatic CCA. 16 with para-aortic metastasis resected.
studies.results: Median survival 33.7 vs 16.7 months (resected vs unresected); not worse than regional node-positive.
studies.limits: Very small; perihilar and distal mixed.
studies.locator: World J Surg 2020 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: Para-aortic data conflict; post-response evidence is limited to a handful of mixed-subsite cases.
questions.certainty: Low for regional nodes after response; very low for non-regional or distant disease.
questions.change: A post-response series of resection with para-aortic or distant disease.

Pooled across three trials 30-day mortality only trended lower with the endoscopic route (RR 0.53, 0.28–1.01). ESGE's own section gives percutaneous drainage higher therapeutic success (OR 3.5) and 11.5-fold less reintervention. Local endoscopic and interventional radiology expertise decides.

questions.title: Tumor size, biopsy history or previously malignant nodes
questions.question: Size, prior biopsy and prior nodes: one exclusion or separate research strata?
questions.context: Review exact radial size, the route of any primary-tumor biopsy, and the full nodal history. These proposed expansions remain closed. Distant or peritoneal disease at any time ends the route.

positions.says: “single and less than three cm in radial (perpendicular to the duct) diameter.” Binding standardized-exception mass wording; historical ≤3 cm study definitions are not identical.
positions.locator: Policy 9.5.A, printed p191; effective 1 October 2026

positions.says: “5/6 (83%) had peritoneal metastases at operative staging.” This was the diagnostic-positive primary-FNA subgroup, not all biopsy-exposed patients.
positions.locator: Published PDF p1 / journal p356, abstract Results

questions.proposal: Keep size expansion, primary transperitoneal-biopsy exposure and cleared malignant nodes as three separate closed transplant strata. Distant or peritoneal metastasis, even after response, ends the transplant route.
rules: For the conventional standardized-exception mass criterion, retain a single mass <3.0 cm in radial diameter. Exactly 3.0 cm is not rounded down; obtain central measurement review. Do not activate a 3–5 cm expansion.

Exclude any prior transperitoneal primary-tumor biopsy exposure from the initial transplanting study. Record trajectory and whether pathology was positive, negative or nondiagnostic; this is a conservative selection rule, not proof of dissemination in every exposed patient.

Exclude previously proven malignant nodes from the initial transplant cohort even after radiographic/pathologic clearance. Nodal EUS sampling that does not traverse the primary is distinct from primary-tumor biopsy. Do not combine these excluded categories in one expansion cohort.

Distant or peritoneal metastasis, or nodal disease beyond the regional field, found at any time (including at operative staging) ends the transplant route for this protocol, even after response to chemoradiation or chemotherapy. There is no proposed stratum.
questions.tests: Original MRI/MRCP or CT with perpendicular radial measurement; full biopsy reports/needle trajectory; node station and original pathology; operative staging plan; resection assessment. Record whether EUS sampled a regional node or traversed the primary mass, the route, pathology result and date. These are not equivalent exposures. Record any distant or peritoneal finding at staging with its pathology.
questions.allocation: Clinical review, standardized exception eligibility and research expansion are separate. A favorable response or living donor does not erase the original size/biopsy/node history.
questions.rationale: Size, biopsy exposure and nodal biology must remain separate. Larger-mass LT has directly unfavorable recurrence data. Biopsy evidence is conflicting across settings, so the mechanism is plausible and current policy is restrictive, but an inevitable-seeding claim is unjustified. No reviewed study validates a cleared-node rescue stratum. Imaging-negative nodes do not equal pathological clearance. Operative staging is where most of this disease is found: in the Mayo series, 36 of 199 patients left the protocol with metastases found at staging (regional nodes 14, intrahepatic 6, extrahepatic 16).
questions.counter: Aveson challenges a universal causal inference from Heimbach. Absence of PM in nine negative TP-FNA cases does not establish safety. Soliman's occult-node recipients do not validate deliberate nodal expansion. One prospective pilot admitted regional lymphadenopathy in locally advanced hilar and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; five of 18 reached transplantation and one had an isolated portacaval nodal recurrence at 12 months. Whether the nodes were proven malignant is not reported in the abstract, and it cannot validate a cleared-node stratum. The exact 3.0-cm boundary is a current policy boundary, not a biological discontinuity proven by these studies.
questions.certainty: Moderate confidence that conventional selection yields better observed outcomes; low certainty for causal effects of size and biopsy; very low/no direct evidence for a previously positive-node clearance pathway.
questions.threshold_basis: POLICY: OPTN 9.5. A specifies radial mass < 3 cm, unresectability, NAT and staging; primary TP-biopsy must be avoided. STUDY: >3 cm associated with lower RFS; positive TP-FNA associated with PM in a very small LT cohort. LOCAL: closing all prior-biopsy and cleared-node strata is a conservative first-study choice, not proof of universal futility.

studies.population: Retrospective 12-US-center NAT-to-LT cohort; 287 entered, 71 dropped out, 214 transplanted. Mostly conventional localized unresectable/PSC-associated pCCA. The expanded subgroup included larger tumors and other departures from eligibility.
studies.results: From treatment-pathway entry, 2-/5-year OS was 68%/53%; post-LT 2-/5-year recurrence-free survival 78%/65%. Among 21 transplanted patients with masses >3 cm, 5-year RFS was 32% versus 69% for smaller tumors. The combined outside-criteria group had recurrence hazard ratio 2.98. Staging found metastases in 17%; four patients were transplanted with metastatic disease, pooled with the outside-criteria group; one centre accepted N0–N1 nodes within the hepatoduodenal ligament. No separate outcome exists for nodal disease.
studies.limits: Larger tumors were not randomized. Composite outside-criteria effect cannot be assigned separately to size, biopsy or metastasis. Small >3-cm recipient subset; selection and center effects.
studies.locator: Gastroenterology 2012; 143: 88–98.e 3; Results, patient flow and selection-criteria recurrence analyses; local full PDF.

studies.population: Mayo 1993–2010; 199 protocol entrants, 62 dropouts, 131 local LT and six elsewhere. Localized unresectable disease; historical size definitions were not identical to current policy.
studies.results: Dropout predictors included >3-cm mass (adjusted HR 2.14, 95% CI 1.08–4.24), CA19-9≥ 500 (HR 2.29), positive/suspicious intraluminal sampling (HR 3.63) and MELD ≥ 20 (HR 3.48). Of 62 dropouts, 36 had metastases found at operative staging (regional nodes 14, intrahepatic 6, extrahepatic 16). Local recipients had 26 recurrences; 5-year OS 71%, RFS 68% from LT.
studies.limits: Strong overlap with Murad multicenter and Heimbach cohorts; not independent replication. These are prognostic associations, not validated universal exclusion thresholds.
studies.locator: Hepatology 2012; 56: 972–981; Tables 2–3 and Transplantation/Recurrence sections.

studies.population: 191 NAT-to-LT protocol entrants; 16 underwent primary-tumor TP-FNA. 13 percutaneous and three EUS primary-tumor biopsies; not EUS nodal staging.
studies.results: Peritoneal metastases at staging: 5/6 with positive TP-FNA versus 14/175 without TP-FNA; 9 negative TP-FNA patients had none; one result was equivocal.
studies.limits: Only six positive biopsies. Nonrandom sampling and more obvious tumor may confound association. Negative-biopsy subgroup is far too small to establish safety or equivalence.
studies.locator: HPB 2011; 13: 356–360; Results and biopsy/staging table; local complete PDF.

studies.population: MSK retrospective planned-resection cohort 1991–2014; 262 patients, 37 TP biopsy versus 225 intraluminal/no biopsy. Resection/exploration setting rather than NAT-to-LT. Median biopsy-to-surgery interval 32 versus 38 days.
studies.results: Peritoneal metastases at surgery 5.4% versus 7.6%; among 243 initially PM-negative patients, 2-year cumulative PM 20.3% versus 20.1%(p=.7).
studies.limits: Direct counterevidence to universal biopsy-seeding claims, but shorter exposure interval, no LT waiting/immunosuppression comparison and only 37 exposed patients. Does not overturn allocation policy.
studies.locator: HPB 2022; 24: 942–949; Methods, Results and cumulative-incidence analysis.

studies.population: Houston recipient-only NAT comparison; 27 LT, 26 analyzed after one treatment-intolerance exclusion. Pre-LT radiological criteria and staging excluded known nodal/extrahepatic disease; six nevertheless had N1/N2 on explant.
studies.results: Occult positive nodes in 6/26(23.1%); nodal disease associated with worse OS and RFS. Nine recurrences overall; main-text 1-/3-year OS 83.0%/52.3% from LT.
studies.limits: Occult nodes discovered after LT are not evidence supporting knowingly positive nodes cleared by therapy. No all referred or all-treated denominator. Abstract/body OS rounding differs; use full Results values.
studies.locator: Transplant Direct 2025; 11: e 1760; Tables 2–4, Recipient Posttransplant Outcomes, Figure 2.

studies.population: Mayo de-novo pCCA 1993–2023; 127 analyzed LT-pathway entrants, 52 dropouts, 75 LT. Protocol staged localized tumors; PSC excluded.

studies.limits: Survival not reported by finding.

questions.title: Resection remains a potentially curative option
questions.question: When is resection a genuine competing curative option?
questions.status: Review the standard treatment · not activated
questions.context: If complete resection may be feasible, compare it with the transplant strategy before entering a transplant study.

positions.says: “If the future liver remnant was insufficient, preoperative portal vein embolization was conducted to enhance hepatic reserve.” Resection optimization is part of the comparator, not a failure of transplant selection.
positions.locator: Published PDF p3 / journal p1130, institutional protocols

positions.says: “>40% for cirrhotic or cholestatic livers” Specialist practice guidance supporting a planning target, not a guaranteed safety threshold.
positions.locator: CIRSE 2024, Table 2; spacing normalized

questions.proposal: Use resection first when an R0 operation and an adequate functional remnant are feasible.
rules: Proposed planning target for cholestatic/cirrhotic liver: FLR/TLV >40%, combined with function, drainage and infection assessment. Volume alone never establishes operative safety; 40% is not an OPTN requirement.

If insufficient remnant is the only barrier, assess selective drainage and augmentation/PVE; reassess remnant volume and function about 2–4 weeks after PVE. Vascular reconstruction or PVE need alone does not prove unresectability.

Return to LT eligibility review only if an R0 resection remains infeasible or unsafe after reasonable optimization. Do not transplant otherwise resectable de novo pCCA outside a specifically approved comparative study.
questions.tests: Two specialist HPB/transplant reviews; vascular/ductal map; CT volumetry; functional assessment where available; cholangitis/drainage status; PVE response and reconstruction plan.
questions.allocation: Policy 9.5.A requires unresectability from technical considerations or underlying liver disease; comparative recipient survival alone does not satisfy this requirement.
questions.rationale: Evidence supports LT as a serious option for carefully selected unresectable pCCA. It does not resolve LT versus feasible optimized R 0 resection. Ethun favors LT even after restricted ITT analysis, whereas Dong loses statistical advantage when dropout is counted. Neither randomization nor comparable entry clocks remove the confounding. PVE can materially change the surgical risk assessment.
questions.counter: Do not cite Dong's nonsignificant ITT p-value as equivalence or proof that resection must always be better. Conversely, recipient-only LT survival cannot erase donor opportunity cost, NAT dropout and wait-list hazards. Reconstructible vascular involvement or a correctable small FLR alone is not proof of permanent unresectability.
questions.certainty: Low comparative certainty; stronger but still nonrandomized evidence for FLR optimization before declaring resection unsafe.
questions.threshold_basis: POLICY: standardized pCCA exception requires unresectability or underlying liver disease. STUDY: PVE growth was assessed at median 22 days in the matched study; comparisons remain observational. GUIDANCE: CIRSE supports higher remnant targets in cholestatic/cirrhotic liver. LOCAL: >40% planning target, reassessment 2–4 weeks and required expert review are workflow proposals; inadequate function/infection can prevent surgery despite adequate volume.

studies.population: Single-center 1993–2023 de-novo pCCA; 288 intended resection (207 resected, 81 dropout) and 127 intended NAT/LT(75 LT, 52 dropout). Resection required attainable R 0 and sufficient FLR; PVE and vascular reconstruction were used. LT recipients were selected for unresectability and conventional tumor biology.
studies.results: As-treated median OS: LT 78 months, resection without vascular resection 58.2, with vascular resection 25.8; 5-year 58.6%, 49.6%, 26.7%. ITT median OS 38.5 months LT versus 31.7 resection (p=.19).
studies.limits: Not equivalence and not proof resection is superior. Historical era, selection and dropout differ. Methods measure LT time from NAT enrollment but resection time from surgery, so even ITT clocks are not perfectly aligned; as-treated LT percentages must not be called purely post-LT.
studies.locator: Hepatology 2026; 1128–1140; Methods Statistics, Figure 1 and OS/ITT analyses; PDFpp 3–8.

studies.population: Multicenter 2000–2015; 234 attempted resections and 70 entered LT protocols; 191 curative-intent resections and 41 confirmed-CCA LT in recipient analysis. LT patients were younger (52 vs 65), more often PSC(61% vs 2%), and more often treated with chemo/RT(98% vs 57%).
studies.results: Recipient 3-/5-year OS 72%/64% LT versus 33%/18% resection. Restricted non-PSC,<3 cm, node-negative comparison favored LT at 5 years 54% vs 29%(p=.03); adjusted/restricted ITT comparison remained significant (p=.049).
studies.limits: Conflicting observational evidence versus Dong; major selection/era/therapy confounding. Exact ITT exclusions and time origin require full-PDF recheck; no unsupported ITT rate is reproduced here.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2018; 267: 797–805; primary abstract and indexed Results/Discussion.

studies.population: 732 consecutive Dutch pCCA presentations 2002–2014; retrospective application of Mayo eligibility. Only 34(5%) potentially LT-eligible after resection/biology/fitness/age screening; not an LT-treated cohort.
studies.results: Without LT, median survival 13 months (95% CI 3–23) from diagnosis/presentation. This shows unmet need among unresectable selected patients, not benefit over R 0 resection.
studies.limits: Historical non-LT care; no matched LT comparator, suspected/confirmed nodes pooled and infection criterion incompletely reconstructible. Abstract 24 PSC versus body 29 PSC inconsistency is irrelevant to the decision and not propagated.
studies.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2021; 28: 1483–1492; Methods Eligibility/Statistical Analyses and Results; complete 10-pagePDF.

studies.population: 20-center retrospective 1667 patients; 1484 combined liver/bile-duct resections analyzed; 298 PVE. Complete-data propensity analysis 98 PVE versus 98 controls. High-risk major resections; exploration-only and LT excluded.
studies.results: Matched PVE versus noPVE: ISGLS B/C liver failure 8% vs 36%; 90-day mortality 7% vs 18%; bile leak 10% vs 35%. Median remnant-volume gain 42% after 22 days.
studies.limits: Unmatched outcomes were worse in PVE patients because they were higher risk. Matching omits unmeasured confounding and excludes missing volumetry; does not prove one FLR cutoff. Operated-only denominator omits patients failing to reach surgery.
studies.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2020; 27: 2311–2318; Methods, Matched Cohort and Table 3; complete 8-pagePDF.

studies.population: 287 NAT/LT entrants across 12 US centers; 214 transplanted. Localized unresectable or PSC-associated disease, not a trial in patients eligible for both R 0 resection and LT.
studies.results: 5-year pathway-entry OS 53% and post-LT RFS 65% are useful feasibility benchmarks, but answer a different question from randomized LT-versus-resection benefit.
studies.limits: Substantial overlap with Mayo comparisons; do not count as an independent comparative test.
studies.locator: Gastroenterology 2012; Results and survival figures; full PDF.

questions.title: Alternative treatment before transplantation
questions.question: May a non-Mayo neoadjuvant regimen replace the conventional program?
questions.status: Alternative regimens not activated · not activated
questions.context: Alternative neoadjuvant regimens require their own approval and cannot be substituted into the standard protocol automatically.

positions.says: “treated with SBRT (50–60 Gy, 3–5 fractions over two weeks)” Small pilot experience supports study development, not noninferiority or interchangeability.
positions.locator: Published PDF p1 abstract; protocol details p3

positions.says: “associated with a higher rate of early hepatic vascular complications” The recurrence signal must be weighed against vascular/graft harm; observational comparison is confounded.
positions.locator: Published PDF p1, abstract Conclusion

questions.proposal: Keep the established Mayo-style pathway as default; develop GemCis-only and SBRT/capecitabine as separately governed alternatives, without claiming equivalence or superiority.
rules: Default to the established fluoropyrimidine/EBRT-based pathway under the approved radiation and pharmacy protocol. Do not treat a pilot dose/fractionation or cycle count as a universal order.

Develop a separately governed prospective GemCis-only feasibility/comparative arm for otherwise conventionally selected pCCA. Retain SBRT/capecitabine as another documented pilot option, not the uniquely evidence-preferred alternative. Neither arm is activated by this document.

Do not combine either alternative with an initial size, primary transperitoneal-biopsy or previously malignant-node expansion. Keep ICI-containing induction outside these initial arms unless separately approved on pre-LT safety evidence.

Before opening, specify regimen delivery, staging, stopping rules, radiation-field and arterial/biliary reconstruction review. Capture every entrant, failure to reach LT, cholangitis, HAT/PVT, biliary injury, graft loss, recurrence and all graft use.
questions.tests: Written radiation/chemotherapy plan and dose modifications; drainage/infection plan; biliary/vascular anatomy; actual prior dose maps; operative staging and graft-safety endpoints.
questions.allocation: Policy requires a written neoadjuvant protocol and operative staging, not this exact regimen. A regimen study does not relax the standardized tumor criteria.
questions.rationale: Conventional fluoropyrimidine-based chemoradiation remains the most mature benchmark. Alternatives have genuine LT evidence, but none has demonstrated noninferiority. The evidence does not justify singling out SBRT as the only acceptable research alternative while categorically closing GemCis-only. Vascular/biliary harm needs prospective surveillance alongside recurrence and dropout.
questions.counter: RT may reduce recurrence yet increase vascular morbidity. Chemo-only favorable selected-recipient outcomes do not reveal who progressed before LT. No-NAT European recipients are not a rationale to omit all induction in a US exception pathway. GCS/RT and SBRT are not interchangeable.
questions.certainty: Moderate confidence in feasibility of conventional selected NAT/LT; very low comparative certainty between named regimens. Direct vascular safety signal deserves action despite nonrandomization.
questions.threshold_basis: POLICY: OPTN requires an approved written protocol including NAT/staging but does not mandate a particular radiation dose. STUDY: SBRT 50–60 Gy/3–5 fractions and GCS/56 Gy are published pilot recipes only. LOCAL: GemCis-only prospective arm, no simultaneous biology expansion, and initial ICI exclusion are risk-management proposals. No validated minimum cycle count or safe vascular dose threshold is inferred.

studies.population: 287 entrants/214 LT across 12 US centers. Localized unresectable/PSC-associated pCCA; 99% EBRT, 98% fluoropyrimidine, 75% brachytherapy.
studies.results: 5-year entry OS 53%; post-LT RFS 65%. No clear RFS difference by brachytherapy receipt was detected.
studies.limits: Strongest mature multi-center pathway benchmark, but no randomized regimen comparison; lack of detected brachytherapy effect does not establish interchangeability.
studies.locator: Gastroenterology 2012; Treatment Characteristics and Outcomes; full PDF.

studies.population: Single-center pilot; 17 evaluated, 12 NAT, 9 listed, 6 LT. Unresectable localized pCCA under historical conventional size/staging criteria.
studies.results: SBRT 50–60 Gy in 3–5 fractions over 2 weeks, followed by capecitabine; 6 LT with 1-year OS 83%.35 pre-LT adverse events and 11 post-LT complications were reported.
studies.limits: Very small feasibility cohort, short oncologic follow-up, no randomized comparator. Regimen is a study description, not a universal radiation prescription or proof SBRT is the preferred alternative.
studies.locator: Liver Transpl 2014; 20: 81–88; Methods, patient flow and adverse-event tables; local PDF.

studies.population: Recipient-only retrospective 2008–2023; 26 analyzed LT, 12 GemCis-only, 14 RT-based including six also receiving GemCis. Localized radiologically eligible pCCA; known metastatic disease excluded.
studies.results: Main-text 1-/3-year OS 83.0%/52.3%; 9/26 recurrences; 1-/3-year RFS 77.8%/59.0%. No statistically significant OS or explant-response difference between treatment strata; RT had more operative blood-loss/transfusion signals.
studies.limits: No pretreatment denominator or differential dropout data; small nonrandom groups, era/selection confounding and occult nodal disease. Supports studying omission, not equivalence. Use main-text values rather than abstract 84%/55%.
studies.locator: Transplant Direct 2025; 11: e 1760; Tables 1–4, Figure 2, Discussion; full PDF.

studies.population: Multicenter 2011–2020; 49 LT, 27 with NAT, 22 without. Similar broad transplant selection but nonrandom center-specific NAT and PSC distributions.
studies.results: Post-LT 5-year OS 41% NAT versus 53% no NAT(not significant); NAT associated with less recurrence (adjusted HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.09–0.97). Major vascular complications 11/27 vs 3/22; hepatic-artery complications 9/27 vs 2/22.
studies.limits: Competing recurrence benefit and treatment harm, not proof RT can routinely be omitted. Abstract 9 vs 2 vascular wording should not replace Table 3's broader 11 vs 3 major-vascular count.
studies.locator: BJSOpen 2023; 7: zrad 025; Table 3, adjusted recurrence analysis and mortality discussion; full PDF.

studies.population: Prospective Kyoto pilot; 10 enrolled, 5 LDLT, 5 dropout. Unresectable localized pCCA; GemCisS 1 induction plus EBRT, typically 56 Gy/28 fractions.
studies.results: All 5 recipients alive at 1 year, median follow-up 23.7 months; one recurrence and 2/5 hepatic-artery thromboses. Dropouts included progression, positive nodes, toxicity/complication, financial withdrawal and one conversion to resection.

shared.proposal: Require 100% completion of the applicable clinical, allocation, donor and research determinations before activation.
rules: Complete six separate dated determinations: clinical suitability; standardized-exception eligibility; nonstandard NLRB review status; calculated-MELD access; LDLT donor clearance; and research authorization. Mark nonapplicable domains explicitly with a reason—do not manufacture six approvals for every patient.
Any required missing, pending or adverse determination is a HOLD. An exception application is not approval, a donor is not recipient benefit, and clinical approval is not study activation.
Recheck the current policy/guidance version before each request; record actual decision and priority rather than predicted entitlement.
shared.tests: Signed suitability record; exact allocation route and policy version; exception outcome; donor-team status; study and institutional activation record.
shared.allocation: Policy 9.4 permits discretionary requests where appropriate; absence of favorable diagnosis-specific guidance is not absence of a review mechanism, and a request does not promise approval.
shared.rationale: The separation is a governance requirement, not an empirical survival cutoff. A clinically appropriate patient can lack exception eligibility, and an approved exception does not prove clinical benefit. LDLT requires an independent donor determination; a registry entry is not permission to perform experimental transplantation.
shared.counter: Not every case needs six separate affirmative approvals: several routes are alternatives or not applicable. An indiscriminate six-approval rule could obstruct appropriate standard care.
shared.certainty: High confidence in the separation of applicable authorities; no trial establishes that six boxes improve survival. Local workflow must map to current institutional obligations.
threshold_basis: Six domains: local checklist architecture, not six mandatory national approvals.
100% applicable completion: governance safeguard, not an outcome-derived percentage.
Hold pending required authorization: operational implementation of separate clinical, donor and research responsibilities.

shared.proposal: Require two independent recipient-benefit reviews and an explicit organ-use case; do not adopt a universal five-year survival cutoff.
rules: Proposed requirements: two reviewers not both responsible for recruitment must document expected incremental benefit over the actual contemporary alternative, with unresolved disagreement referred to the full committee.

For DDLT, show local expected access/dropout and sensitivity scenarios at 6, 12 and 18 months, total graft use including retransplantation, and plausible alternative recipients. These are planning scenarios, not imposed waiting periods.

For LDLT, separately show healthy-donor risk and potential downstream deceased-donor graft use. Do not call DCD, extended-criteria grafts or machine perfusion “zero opportunity cost.” No priority changes follow from an AI-selected survival threshold.
shared.tests: Same-eligibility/time-zero comparator; expected access; dropout; donor/graft type; uncertainty intervals; graft loss/retransplant estimate; written independent reviews.
shared.allocation: Only the applicable allocation process determines priority. Favorable post-LT prognosis, evidence grade and urgency are not interchangeable measures.
shared.rationale: Use pathway-level benefit from an agreed entry date, not recipient-only survival. Compare with contemporary tumor-specific care and actual local access. LDLT avoids one direct deceased-donor allocation but creates healthy-donor risk and may generate rescue graft use. Graft quality/perfusion changes do not make opportunity cost zero.
shared.counter: An ambitious prognosis threshold can exclude patients with substantial incremental benefit, while an indolent tumor can have excellent post-LT survival and little incremental benefit. Local wait times and unequal access can reverse a study’s apparent advantage.
shared.certainty: Benefit evidence differs by disease: randomized selected CRLM/HCC pathways cannot be generalized to all expanded indications. Ethical principles are authoritative frameworks, not empirically optimized allocation weights.
threshold_basis: Two reviewers: local independence safeguard, not validated optimum.
6/12/18 months: sensitivity scenarios for access/dropout, not mandatory waits.
HCC ≥60% five-year ITT OS: one expert trial-design benchmark; not a cross-cancer allocation policy.
All grafts: count initial and rescue/retransplant grafts; donor morbidity remains a separate outcome.

studies.results: From randomization, five-year overall survival was 77.5% with LT versus 31.2% without LT; tumor-event-free survival 76.8% versus 18.3%; median follow-up 71 months.
studies.limits: Strongest causal evidence for LT among selected responders, not for all 74 entrants or unlimited initial burden. Small, prematurely stopped trial. studies.population: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression. Age 18–65; ECOG 0–1; R0 colorectal primary; BRAF nonmutated; no prior or current extrahepatic disease/local recurrence; chemotherapy response or stable disease for at least 3 months, at most three lines. CEA <80 ng/mL OR at least 50% reduction from peak was permitted. Independent committee of at least two surgeons, two oncologists and one radiologist reviewed original and current lesion maps. These are trial criteria, not identical to current NLRB guidance.
studies.results: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.
studies.limits: Strong evidence for the selected trial population, not for BRAF-mutant, ECOG 2, active extrahepatic, truly NED, resectable or broadly expanded disease. PP survival conditions on reaching treatment and must not replace ITT. The Results recurrence denominator is 26/36; Figure 3 caption says 28 recurrences, consistent with a broader all-grafted report, so do not mix these denominators. QoL collection had only 55/74 per-protocol baseline questionnaires and is descriptive, not proof of a large QoL gain. Priority allocation and rapid access were part of the treatment strategy.

rules: Proposed readiness requirements: independent donor evaluation/advocacy, documented freedom to withdraw, recipient-benefit uncertainty consent, and funded medical, psychological, recovery and financial follow-up before investigational LDLT.

Proposed local follow-up: baseline, six weeks, six months, one year, two years, then annually through five years. Meet current OPTN reporting duties separately; this five-year support plan is not claimed to be a national reporting requirement.

One donor death, life-threatening complication, permanent major disability or liver failure requiring transplantation triggers an immediate pause of the relevant investigational LDLT activity and independent review. Other serious donor harm also warrants review; reopening needs independent authorization.
shared.tests: Graft/resection-specific and center-specific risk; donor recovery/employment baseline; independent consent and advocate records; funded follow-up/support; sentinel-event response owner.
shared.allocation: LDLT clearance is separate from recipient selection; the potential need for retransplantation must be included in organ-use discussions.
shared.rationale: Donor mortality is low but not zero; complication, recovery and financial burdens are more frequent. Registry missingness and selected healthy donors limit reassurance. Consent must include uncertain recipient benefit, recurrence and possible early graft loss, without pressure to proceed or relax donor criteria.
shared.counter: Older A2ALL complication rates and modern SRTR mortality are different outcomes from overlapping eras/cohorts; do not pool them. shared.certainty: Moderate certainty for the existence of material donor burden; lower certainty for individual risk and long-term recovery because of incomplete follow-up. No oncology-specific randomized donor-safety comparison.
threshold_basis: Baseline/6 weeks/6 months/1/2 years then annually to five: proposed support schedule; current mandatory reporting remains separately checked.
One sentinel event: conservative review/pause trigger, not a statistically estimated harm boundary.
No relaxed donor criteria: protection against shifting uncertain recipient benefit onto a healthy person.

shared.proposal: Use a small staged pilot with all-screened accounting and explicit safety pauses; no automatic expansion on favorable recipient survival.
rules: Proposed initial cap: ten transplants per separately approved biological stratum. Review after the first five have 90-day follow-up; no expansion decision until all first ten have at least 12-month follow-up. Reconcile vital status, graft events and known serious harms for every participant; require ≥90% completeness for other prespecified key outcomes.

In an initial experimental cohort, one all-cause recipient death, graft loss or retransplantation within 90 days triggers a pause of further experimental enrollment/transplantation pending independent review. A later possibly treatment-related death/graft loss or a donor sentinel event also triggers review/pause. Rescue care is never withheld; reopening requires independent authorization.

These are proposed conservative review triggers, not statistically validated efficacy/futility boundaries. Before opening, biostatistics and the independent board must ratify or replace them with indication-specific rules, denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria.

Capture every screened candidate, including nonrecipients, conversion to resection, dropout, deaths and access barriers; report survival from entry and from LT, recurrence, graft use, donor recovery and quality of life. Ten survivors alone do not establish benefit or authorize expansion.
shared.tests: Locked eligibility strata; prospective entry/time-zero dataset; modern comparator; adverse-event definitions; follow-up-completeness report; independently signed statistical and safety plan.
shared.allocation: Study monitoring never changes exception criteria or guarantees future access. Audit access by referral, geography, resources and donor availability without turning protected characteristics into exclusion rules.
shared.rationale: A small pilot can test feasibility, staging fidelity, data capture and acute safety, not prove durable survival benefit. Define time zero, all-screened enrollment, waitlist failures, post-LT survival/recurrence, competing death, all grafts, donor harms and patient-reported outcomes before opening. An independent board needs actual pause/reopening authority.
shared.counter: Zero observed events among ten fully followed independent patients still has a one-sided exact 95% binomial upper bound of 25.9% (1−0.05^(1/10)). Thus ten survivors cannot establish a <5% event risk. Ninety percent data completeness permits one missing patient; safety events and vital status require active ascertainment, not tolerance of unaccounted loss.
shared.certainty: Strong methodological rationale for predefinition and ITT accounting; no empirical validation of our exact cap/interim/completeness thresholds. Late recurrence demands multi-year follow-up.
threshold_basis: Ten per stratum and interim after five at 90 days: local feasibility cap and safety review cadence.

≥90%: proposed non-vital key-measure completeness threshold; not permission to ignore deaths/graft events or unknown status.
One early death/graft loss/re-LT: review/pause trigger, not automatic futility or withholding rescue.
